optimizers7

Almost every R package that fits a model carries its own optimizer, written inside the function that needs it: a loop, a while (!converged), a tolerance compared with a quantity chosen by the author. Such an optimizer cannot be reused or extended outside the package, and it provides only the quantities that its author needed. The stopping rule, which defines what the procedure means by finished, is usually a constant deep inside the code.

In optimizers7, each optimizer is written once, as an object. An optimizer carries its algorithm and every setting of that algorithm; a stopping rule is a separate object that can be replaced, combined, or written by the user; and every algorithm is written once against one interface for the objective.

The package minimizes the function that it is given, and it does not represent observations, the origin of the data or the meaning of the parameters. Those belong to the calling package.

It is the optimization layer of statmodels7, alongside linkfunctions7 and distributions7.

Installation 

# install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("statmodels7/optimizers7")

To install the whole toolkit, including the other packages of the toolkit, use:

pak::pak("statmodels7/statmodels7")

Minimizing a function

Every algorithm minimizes, through one generic:

f  <- function(p) 100 * (p[2] - p[1]^2)^2 + (1 - p[1])^2
gr <- function(p) c(-400 * p[1] * (p[2] - p[1]^2) - 2 * (1 - p[1]),
                    200 * (p[2] - p[1]^2))

minimize(bfgs(), f, par = c(-1.2, 1), gr = gr)
#> <optimizer_result> BFGS
#>   value      : 3.21085e-13
#>   par        : 1 1
#>   iterations : 35   evaluations: f 49, g 39
#>   elapsed    : 0 us
#>   converged  : yes (gradient (max-norm) < 1e-06 or |df| < 1e-10 or |dx| < 1e-08)

Changing the algorithm changes one word, because every optimizer carries the same shared settings:

minimize(lbfgs(), f, c(-1.2, 1), gr = gr)@par
#> [1] 1 1
minimize(newton(), f, c(-1.2, 1), gr = gr)@par
#> [1] 1 1
minimize(nelder_mead(), f, c(-1.2, 1))@par
#> [1] 1 1

Stopping rules

A rule written inside an algorithm fixes the meaning of convergence when the package is written. Here a rule is an object:

crit_any(crit_grad(1e-10), crit_rel_obj(1e-14))
#> <criterion> gradient (max-norm) < 1e-10 or |df| < 1e-14 (relative)

Rules compose, and a new rule is one class and one method:

CritTiny <- S7::new_class("CritTiny", parent = criterion,
                          properties = list(tol = S7::class_numeric))
S7::method(crit_met, CritTiny) <- function(criterion, state)
  state$f_new < criterion@tol

minimize(bfgs(criterion = CritTiny(label = "f < 1e-8", tol = 1e-8)),
         f, c(-1.2, 1), gr = gr)@criterion_met
#> [1] "f < 1e-8"

A rule that an optimizer cannot evaluate is rejected when the run starts, with an error that names the missing quantity, instead of being accepted and never firing:

minimize(nelder_mead(criterion = crit_grad()), f, c(-1.2, 1))
#> Error:
#> ! The stopping rule needs gradient, which nelder-mead does not provide.
#>   Choose a criterion this optimizer can evaluate, or a method that provides it.

Bounds by reparametrization

Each bounded coordinate is reparametrized onto the whole real line, so every proposed point is admissible by construction: there is no rejection step and no boundary for a line search to cross, and a method needs no code of its own for bounds. The exception is prox_grad(), which takes its constraint through its proximal operator and rejects lower and upper:

y <- rnorm(200, mean = 0, sd = 2)
nll <- function(p) length(y) * log(p) + sum(y^2) / (2 * p^2)

minimize(bfgs(), nll, par = 1, lower = 0)@par
#> [1] 1.854906
sqrt(mean(y^2))
#> [1] 1.854906

Starting values that need not be written out

par may be a starter instead of a vector. Both starters work on the unconstrained scale and are mapped back through the bounds. On that scale one constant suits every kind of parameter, since zero becomes one for a variance and one half for a probability, and every draw lies inside its box:

X <- cbind(1, matrix(rnorm(60), 30))
b <- drop(X %*% c(0.5, -1, 2)) + rnorm(30, sd = 0.2)
rss <- function(p) sum((b - X %*% p)^2)

minimize(bfgs(), rss, start_zeros())@par        # how many? worked out
#> [1]  0.5175641 -1.0649279  1.9870314
minimize(bfgs(), rss, start_runif(-2, 2))@par   # or drawn, on that scale
#> [1]  0.5175641 -1.0649279  1.9870314

The number of parameters is given by start_zeros(npar = 3), by bounds with one element per parameter, or, as above, by the objective itself, probed once before the run. X %*% p with a parameter of the wrong length is an error and not a number, so an objective written as a matrix product determines the length. A vectorized expression that accepts several lengths does not, and the probe then raises an error that names the lengths accepted.

Objectives without a derivative at the minimum

A descent method reaches the minimum of a sum of absolute deviations and then reports that it did not converge. The report is correct, because the subgradient that it evaluates near the minimum has norm 1 and does not become small. bundle() keeps a collection of subgradients and tests whether zero lies in their convex hull, which is the condition that holds at the minimizer:

z <- rnorm(101)
sad <- function(p) sum(abs(z - p))
sub <- function(p) -sum(sign(z - p))

c(bfgs   = minimize(bfgs(), sad, par = 0, gr = sub)@converged,
  bundle = minimize(bundle(), sad, par = 0, gr = sub)@converged)
#>   bfgs bundle 
#>  FALSE   TRUE

c(bundle = minimize(bundle(), sad, par = 0, gr = sub)@par, median = median(z))
#>     bundle     median 
#> 0.06462703 0.06462703

Components of the package

second order newton(), bfgs(), lbfgs()
third order chebyshev()
first order cg(), bb(), gd()
noisy objectives, and long parameter vectors adam()
no derivative nelder_mead(), compass()
one parameter brent()
global search sa()
non-smooth, with subgradients bundle()
non-smooth, with a proximal operator prox_grad()
wrappers multistart(), parallel by default, and chain()
line searches armijo(), wolfe(), nonmonotone()
starting values start_zeros(), start_runif()
stopping rules crit_grad(), crit_abs_obj(), crit_rel_obj(), crit_abs_par(), crit_rel_par(), crit_stationary(), crit_never(), and crit_any() / crit_all() to combine them

Every method counts its own evaluations, records in its trace the safeguards that fired, and sets converged only when the run ended on its stopping rule (or on the resolution of the objective), never because a budget ran out.

multistart() runs its starts in parallel without any setup: ncores is a number, by default as many processes as there are starts and at most the number of cores minus two. The call itself starts the workers, loads the package on them, gives each of them an independent random stream and shuts them down. The implementation uses forks on Linux and macOS and a socket cluster on Windows. For a deterministic optimizer such as bfgs(), set.seed() reproduces the run identically however many cores were used; for a stochastic one such as sa() the result depends on ncores.

Validating an optimizer

check_optimizer() runs twelve checks on what an optimizer reports: that value is the objective at par, that a reported gradient is the gradient there, that bounds hold strictly, that a run repeats, and others. It then reports, separately, the gaps that the method reached on the standard test problems; these gaps measure performance and do not enter the verdicts:

check_optimizer(bfgs())
#> Checking optimizer: BFGS
#>   [ 1] value agrees with par:            [PASSED]
#>   [ 2] gradient agrees with par:         [PASSED]
#>   [ 3] convergence is not assumed:       [PASSED]
#>   [ 4] budgets are respected:            [PASSED]
#>   [ 5] evaluations are counted:          [PASSED]
#>   [ 6] trace is well formed:             [PASSED]
#>   [ 7] bounds are respected strictly:    [PASSED]
#>   [ 8] the run repeats:                  [PASSED]
#>   [ 9] maximize mirrors minimize:        [PASSED]
#>   [10] an unevaluable rule is rejected:  [PASSED]
#>   [11] a bad starting point is an error: [PASSED]
#>   [12] it minimizes a quadratic:         [PASSED]
#> 
#>   All checks passed.
#> 
#>   battery (gap from the known minimum; information, not a verdict)
#>     sphere       gap  4.62e-33  conv        3 evals  
#>     rosenbrock   gap  3.21e-13  conv       49 evals  
#>     booth        gap  1.73e-17  conv        8 evals  
#>     beale        gap  3.18e-15  conv       17 evals  
#>     powell       gap  4.28e-11  conv       39 evals  
#>     himmelblau   gap  6.27e-14  conv       17 evals  multimodal
#>     rastrigin    gap  0.00e+00  conv       11 evals  multimodal
#>     abs_sum      gap  1.26e-02  -          84 evals  non-smooth
